questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The degeneracy of hydrogen atom that has energy equal to $\frac{-R_{\mathrm{H}}}{9}$ is (where, $R_{\mathrm{H}}=$ Rydberg constant)
questions.solution:
The energy is given as, $E=-\frac{R_{\mathrm{H}}}{9}...(i)$
We know that,
$\begin{aligned}
E_n & =-\frac{R_{\mathrm{H}}}{n^2}...(ii)\\
n^2 & =9 \\
n & =3
\end{aligned}$
When $n=3, l=0,1,2(3 s, 3 p, 3 d \text{ sub-shells) } 
Orbitals present (i.e., degeneracy),
$3 s=1,3 p=3,3 d=5$
Total number of orbital present $=3+1+5=9

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If the de-broglie wavelength of a particle of mass $(m)$ is 100 times its velocity. Then, its value in terms of its mass $(m)$ and plank constant $(h)$ is
questions.solution:
Let the wavelength of given particle $=x$
Velocity $(v)=\frac{x}{100}$
Using wavelength formula
$\begin{aligned} \lambda = \frac{h}{m v} \\
\therefore & x =\frac{h}{m\left(\frac{x}{100}\right)} \\
x & =\frac{100 h}{m x} \\
x^2 & =100 \frac{h}{m} \\
\Rightarrow \quad x & =10 \sqrt{\frac{h}{m}}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The wavelength corresponding to maximum energy for hydrogen is $91. 2nm$. The corresponding wavelength for ${He}^{+}$ ion is
questions.solution:
Accordinq to Rydberg's equation

$\overset{¯}{v} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = {RZ}^{2}\left[1{n}_{L}^{2} - 1{n}_{H}^{2}\right]$

where,

$\overset{¯}{v} =$ wave number

$\lambda =$ wavelength

$R =$ Rydberg constant $\left(= 109677{cm}^{- 1}\right)$

$Z =$ atomic number

${n}_{L} =$ lower energy state

${n}_{H} =$ higher energy state.

i.e. $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} ∝ {Z}^{2}$

Thus, $\dfrac{\lambda\left({He}^{+}\right)}{\lambda\left(H\right)} = \dfrac{{Z}^{2}\left(H\right)}{{Z}^{2}\left({He}^{+}\right)}$

To find $\lambda\left({He}^{+}\right) = ?$

Given, $\lambda\left(H\right) = 91 . 2nm$

$Z\left(H\right) = 1$

$Z\left(He\right) = 2$

$∴ \lambda\left({He}^{+}\right) = \dfrac{1 \times 91 . 2}{4} = 22 . 8nm$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: If the photon of wavelength $150$ pm strikes an atom and one of its inner bound electron is ejected out with a velocity of $1. 5 \times {10}^{7}m / s$,& what is the energy with which it is bound to the nucleus?
questions.solution:
Total energy $\left(E\right)$ of any photon is given by the relation : $E = \dfrac{hc}{λ}$

Where, $h =$ Planck's constant $= 6 . 6 \times {10}^{- 34}Js$

$c =$ Velocity of light $= 3 \times {10}^{8}m / s$

$\lambda =$ wavelength $= 1 . 5 \times {10}^{- 10}m,$ i.e, $\left(150pm\right)$

Thus, $E = \dfrac{hc}{λ} = \dfrac{6 . 6 \times {10}^{- 34} \times 3 \times {10}^{8}}{1 . 5 \times {10}^{- 10}}; E = 1 . 32 \times {10}^{- 15}J$ and, energy of ejected electron $\left(E^{'}\right)$

$E^{'} = \dfrac{1}{2}{mv}^{2}$,

where,

$m =$ mass of electron $= 9 . 1 \times {10}^{- 31}kg$

$v =$ velocity of electron

$= 1 . 5 \times {10}^{7}m / s$

$E^{'} = \dfrac{1}{2}{mv}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 . 1 \times {10}^{- 31} \times \left(1 . 5 \times {10}^{7}\right)2$

$E^{'} = 1 . 024 \times {10}^{- 16}$

Thus, total energy of photon $=$ Binding energy of electron

$\left(B\right)$ + energy of ejected electron $\left(E^{'}\right)$

Thus, $1 . 32 \times {10}^{- 15} = \left(B\right) + \left($ E\right)$

$∴ $\left($ B\right) = $\left($ E\right) - $\left($ E^{'}\right) = $\left[1 . 32 \times {10}^{- 15}\right] - \left[1 . 024 \times {10}^{- 16}\right]$

$= 1 . 2176 \times {10}^{- 15}J$

$= \dfrac{1 . 2176 \times {10}^{- 15}}{1 . 6 \times {10}^{- 19}}$ eV = 7 . 6 \times {10}^{3}eV$

$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In an atom, an electron is moving with a speed of $600m / s$ with an accuracy of $0. 005 %$. Certainty with which the position of the electron can be located is (h = 6. 6 \times {10}^{- 34}kgm^{2}s^{- 1}$, mass of electron, ${m}_{e} = 9. 1 \times {10}^{- 31}kg$)$
questions.solution:
Given that velocity of electron, $v = 600m / s$

Accuracy of velocity $= 0.005%$

According to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

$\left(\Delta x\right) . \left(m \Delta v\right) = \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$

$∆ v = 0 . 005 %$~or& $600ms^{- 1}$

$= \dfrac{600 \times 0 . 005}{100} = 0 . 03$

$∆ x \times 9 . 1 \times {10}^{- 31} \times 0 . 03 = \dfrac{6 . 6 \times {10}^{- 34}}{4 \times 3 . 14}$

Hence,~$∆ x = \dfrac{6 . 6 \times {10}^{- 34}}{4 \times 3 . 14 \times 0 . 03 \times 9 . 1 \times {10}^{- 31}}$

$= 1 . 92 \times {10}^{- 3}m$
